lesson.title: Reading Family Trees Like a Geneticist
lesson.summary: A pedigree is a diagram of a family's inheritance history that geneticists use to trace how a trait is passed down and to determine whether it follows an autosomal or sex-linked, dominant or recessive pattern.
lesson.body:
Not every genetic cross can be arranged in a laboratory. For human traits and disorders, geneticists instead work backward from the offspring that already exist, using a pedigree, a standardized diagram of a family tree. By convention, squares represent males and circles represent females, a horizontal line connecting a square and a circle represents a mating pair, and vertical lines connect parents to their children, arranged left to right in birth order along a horizontal line for each generation. A filled in symbol indicates an individual who shows the trait or disorder being studied, while an open symbol indicates an individual who does not.

Reading a pedigree means applying the same logic used in monohybrid crosses and Punnett squares, just in reverse. Instead of predicting offspring ratios from known parental genotypes, the pedigree gives the actual offspring, and the question is what parental genotypes, and what mode of inheritance, could have produced that pattern. This is essentially a test cross performed by nature: an affected child born to two unaffected parents is very informative, because it tells you both of those unaffected parents must be carriers of a recessive allele, exactly as an unexpected recessive phenotype among the offspring of a test cross reveals a heterozygous parent.

The pattern across generations helps distinguish dominant from recessive traits. A recessive trait can skip generations entirely, appearing in a grandchild whose grandparent also had it, without showing up in the carrier parent in between, and it tends to require both parents to at least carry the allele. A dominant trait essentially never skips a generation, since every affected individual should have inherited the dominant allele from at least one affected parent, aside from the rare case of a brand new mutation. Distinguishing autosomal from sex-linked inheritance depends on whether the trait shows up equally in males and females or is skewed toward one sex, and on whether fathers pass the trait to their sons, which is impossible for an X-linked trait since fathers give a Y chromosome, not an X, to every son.

Consider a concrete case. Two unaffected parents have a daughter who is affected by some trait. Could this be X-linked recessive. For a daughter to show an X-linked recessive trait, she must be homozygous recessive on the X chromosome, meaning she needed to receive a recessive allele from both parents, including her father. But a father only has one X chromosome, so if he is unaffected, his single X carries the dominant allele, and that is the only X he can give to a daughter. An unaffected father therefore cannot produce an affected daughter for an X-linked recessive trait. Since the daughter in this pedigree is affected despite having an unaffected father, X-linked recessive inheritance is ruled out, and autosomal recessive inheritance, with both unaffected parents as carriers, becomes the best explanation. This kind of elimination, testing each mode of inheritance against the actual pattern in the pedigree, is the core skill of pedigree analysis.
